title: Least generic formal singular height controls low-height excellence in arbitrary characteristic
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian normal Nagata domain [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-weil-pbc-normal-ring, def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring]. Let $0\ne x\in R$ be a nonunit, and suppose $R$ is $(x)$-adically complete [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring], universally catenary, not quasi-excellent, with every quotient $R/K$ for a nonzero ideal $K$ quasi-excellent [def-exc-excellent-ring]. For each finite extension $L/\operatorname{Frac}R$, let $B_L$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Assume that $B_L$ is finite as an $R$-module, normal, Nagata, universally catenary and $(x)$-adically complete, that $B_L/xB_L$ is quasi-excellent, and that the maximal-ideal completion $\widehat{(B_L)_{\mathfrak n}}$ is a normal local domain for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$ of $B_L$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime, def-weil-pbc-adic-completion].

For each such $L,\mathfrak n$, put $C_{L,\mathfrak n}=\varprojlim_j (B_L)_{\mathfrak n}/x^j(B_L)_{\mathfrak n}$. For a Noetherian ring $T$, write $\operatorname{Sing}(T)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}T:T_{\mathfrak p}\text{ is not regular local}\}$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-regular-scheme]. A minimal singular prime is a member of this set containing no strictly smaller member. Define
$$\mathcal S=\{(L,\mathfrak n,\mathfrak s):\mathfrak s\text{ is a minimal singular prime of }C_{L,\mathfrak n},\ \mathfrak s\cap B_L=(0)\}.$$
Height means $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=\dim T_{\mathfrak p}$, with Krull dimension as in [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Then every $C_{L,\mathfrak n}$ is a Noetherian normal local G-ring [def-weil-pbc-g-ring], and its singular locus is closed. The set $\mathcal S$ is nonempty. Its heights have a least value $h\in\mathbf N$ with $h\geq2$, attained by some triple in $\mathcal S$. Every $R_{\mathfrak p}$ with $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p\leq h$, and every $(B_L)_{\mathfrak q}$ with $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q\leq h$, is excellent.

source.place: Kurano–Shimomoto, Ideal-adic completion of quasi-excellent rings (after Gabber), Theorem 5.1, Step 2, (5.1)–(5.6) and Claim 5.2, pp.9–11; low-height finite-normalization consequence on p.13. No characteristic hypothesis. Read online; local bibliographic copy WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: Fix $L,\mathfrak n$, and abbreviate $B=B_L$, $A=B_{\mathfrak n}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak nA$, $C=C_{L,\mathfrak n}$. A finite module algebra is finite type (its module generators also generate it as an algebra). Hence $B$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian], $A$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian], and $C$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-adic-completion-noetherian]. By [lem-weil-pbc-adic-complete-jacobson-radical], $x$ belongs to every maximal ideal of $B$, so $x\in\mathfrak m$. By [lem-weil-pbc-adic-completion-mod-ideal], $C$ is $xC$-adically complete and $C/xC=A/xA$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, construction preceding (5.1), printed p.9; Stacks 0316, 05GI, 05GG.

proof.text: The quotient $C/xC=A/xA$ is local and $xC$ is in the Jacobson radical by [lem-weil-pbc-adic-complete-jacobson-radical]. Thus $C$ is local, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak mC$, and $A\to C$ is local. For each $j\geq1$, exact completion of $0\to\mathfrak m^j\to A\to A/\mathfrak m^j\to0$, together with its finite-module tensor description, gives $C/\mathfrak m^jC\cong(A/\mathfrak m^j)^{\wedge(x)}=A/\mathfrak m^j$: the last completion stabilizes because $x^j\in\mathfrak m^j$. These isomorphisms are induced by $A\to C$, hence commute with all quotient transitions. Taking inverse limits identifies $\widehat C=\widehat A$, compatibly with the maps from $A$ and $C$. This is a short quotient calculation, not an extra completion theorem.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, common maximal-adic completion in (5.3), printed p.9; quotient calculation using Stacks 00MB and 00MA.

proof.text: By [lem-per-quasi-excellent-localization], $A/xA$ is quasi-excellent, since it is a localization of the assumed quasi-excellent ring $B/xB$. In particular it is a G-ring. Apply [lem-per-local-g-ring-adic-lifting] to the local complete pair $(C,xC)$ from steps 1–2: $C$ is a G-ring. Apply [lem-per-semilocal-g-ring-j2] to this local ring: it is quasi-excellent and therefore has closed singular locus. The map $C\to\widehat C=\widehat A$ is regular by [lem-weil-pbc-g-ring-completion-regular] and faithfully flat by [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-faithfully-flat]. The target is a normal local domain by the assumption on the maximal-adic completion of $(B_L)_{\mathfrak n}$. Hence [lem-sfb-faithfully-flat-normal-ring-descent] makes $C$ normal; as a local normal ring it is a domain. This proves every assertion about each individual $C_{L,\mathfrak n}$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, (5.1) and (5.3), printed p.9; local lifting theorem and semilocal G-ring assertion in Section 2.

proof.text: We record why only generic formal fibres can fail. For primes $0\ne\mathfrak t\subseteq\mathfrak p$ of $R$, $R/\mathfrak t$ is quasi-excellent by hypothesis; its localization at $\mathfrak p/\mathfrak t$ is quasi-excellent by [lem-per-quasi-excellent-localization]. Its completion map is regular by [lem-weil-pbc-g-ring-completion-regular]. The generic fibre of that map is geometrically regular, and [lem-weil-pbc-formal-fibre-quotient-iso] identifies it with the fibre over $\mathfrak t$ of $R_{\mathfrak p}\to\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}$. Thus all nonzero-prime fibres of every such completion map are geometrically regular.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, first paragraph and Claim 5.2 first paragraph, printed pp.9–10; Stacks 07PN.

proof.text: The quotient $R/xR$ is quasi-excellent since $xR\ne0$, and $xR$ is in the Jacobson radical by [lem-weil-pbc-adic-complete-jacobson-radical]. If $R$ were a G-ring, [lem-per-g-ring-quasi-excellent-closed-fibre] would make it quasi-excellent, contrary to hypothesis. By [lem-weil-pbc-g-ring-maximal-ideal-criterion], choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ whose local completion map is not regular. It is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-faithfully-flat], so step 4 shows that its generic fibre $F=K\otimes_R\widehat{R_{\mathfrak m}}$, $K=\operatorname{Frac}R$, is not geometrically regular. This ring is Noetherian: it is a localization of a Noetherian completion. By [def-weil-pbc-g-ring], there is a finite purely inseparable extension $L/K$ such that $L\otimes_K F$ is not regular. This includes the degree-one extension; no characteristic assumption is used.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, first paragraph, printed p.9, using Theorem 4.1; finite purely inseparable test expanded from the definition.

proof.text:
For any finite extension $L/K$ put $B=B_L$. Then $(R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}B=L$: given $z\in L$, choose a monic equation $z^r+\sum_{i<r}a_i z^i=0$ over $K$ and a common nonzero denominator $d\in R$ for the $a_i$. The equation for $dz$ has coefficients $d^{r-i}a_i\in R$, so $dz\in B$ and $z=(dz)/d$. For any prime $\mathfrak p$ of $R$, apply [lem-weil-pbc-completion-finite-extension] to the finite $R$-algebra $B$, then invert all nonzero elements of $B$, using [lem-weil-pbc-localization-base-change] and [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-cancel-base-change]. It gives
$$L\otimes_K(K\otimes_R\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}})\cong\prod_{\mathfrak q\cap R=\mathfrak p}\bigl(L\otimes_B\widehat{B_{\mathfrak q}}\bigr).$$
The product is finite. A finite product is regular exactly when each factor is regular: a prime selects one factor (the coordinate idempotents are orthogonal and sum to one), its local ring is that factor's local ring, and a finite product is Noetherian exactly when its factors are. These are componentwise ideal and localization calculations. This is the scalar identity used in the source's two cofiber squares.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, the two cofiber squares on printed pp.9–10; Stacks 07N9, lemma-completion-finite-extension, with scalar identities expanded.

proof.text: Apply step 6 to the $L$ and $\mathfrak m$ chosen in step 5. Since its left side is not regular, some factor $L\otimes_B\widehat{B_{\mathfrak n}}$, for a prime $\mathfrak n$ of $B$ over $\mathfrak m$, is not regular; $\mathfrak n$ is a maximal ideal by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-prime-over-maximal-maximal], since $B$ is integral over $R$ and $\mathfrak m$ is maximal. Put $C=C_{L,\mathfrak n}$. If $L\otimes_B C$ were regular, every local ring of $\widehat{B_{\mathfrak n}}$ at a prime over $(0)\subset B$ would be regular: the corresponding local ring of $C$ is regular, and the local map is flat with regular closed fibre because $C\to\widehat C=\widehat{B_{\mathfrak n}}$ is regular (step 3). Apply [lem-weil-pbc-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre]. This contradicts the chosen factor. Thus $L\otimes_B C$ is not regular, and has a singular prime, corresponding to a singular prime of $C$ contracting to zero in $B$. Since $\operatorname{Sing}C$ is closed, write it as $V(J)$; [lem-weil-pbc-prime-contains-minimal-prime] supplies a prime minimal over $J$ below that singular prime. Its contraction to $B$ is still zero. It therefore gives a member of $\mathcal S$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, definition of S_L and (5.2), printed p.9.

proof.text: Every prime in each Noetherian $C$ has finite natural height by [lem-trf-noetherian-prime-finite-height]. The nonempty set of these natural heights therefore has a least element $h$, realized by a triple. Each $C$ is normal by step 3, hence satisfies $(R_1)$ by [lem-weil-pbc-serre-criterion-normal]. By the definition of $(R_1)$ in [def-weil-pbc-serre-conditions-rk-sk], a singular prime cannot have height zero or one. Hence $h\geq2$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, (5.2)–(5.4), printed p.9; Stacks 031S and 0BBZ.

proof.text: Fix $0\ne\mathfrak p\subset R$ with $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p\leq h$, and let $L/K$ be any finite extension. Put $B=B_L$ and take any prime $\mathfrak q$ of $B$ over $\mathfrak p$. By [lem-exc-dimension-formula-universally-catenary-finite-type-domain], $0<\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p\leq h$: both the fraction-field and residue-field extensions are algebraic. Choose a maximal $\mathfrak n\supseteq\mathfrak q$ and put $C=C_{L,\mathfrak n}$, $A=B_{\mathfrak q}$. The map $B_{\mathfrak n}\to C$ is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-completion-flat] and local by step 2, hence faithfully flat by [lem-pc-local-flat-faithful-flat-reflects-surjective]. Thus $\mathfrak qC$ is proper: [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-surjective-spectrum] gives a prime over $\mathfrak qB_{\mathfrak n}$. Choose $Q$ minimal over $\mathfrak qC$ using [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-prime-over-proper-ideal]. Its contraction to $B$ equals $\mathfrak q$, since otherwise [lem-sc-flat-going-down] would produce a smaller prime over $\mathfrak q$ still containing $\mathfrak qC$. The flat local map $\alpha:A\to C_Q$ has zero-dimensional closed fibre, since $Q$ is minimal over $\mathfrak qC$. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-flat-height-formula] gives $\operatorname{ht}Q=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q\leq h$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, Claim 5.2, (5.5)–(5.6), printed p.10; Stacks 02IJ, 00HS and 00ON.

proof.text: Put $T=\widehat{C_Q}$. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian] and [lem-weil-pbc-adic-completion-noetherian], these local rings are Noetherian. The map $\widehat\alpha:\widehat A\to T$ is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-completion], and it is local since the compatible completion map carries the extended maximal ideal of $A$ into that of $C_Q$; the description of these maximal ideals is [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-local-ring]. It is faithfully flat by [lem-pc-local-flat-faithful-flat-reflects-surjective]. Since $C$ is a G-ring, the map $C_Q\to T$ is regular by [def-weil-pbc-g-ring].

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, Claim 5.2, diagram alpha, beta and completed alpha, printed p.10; Stacks 0C4G and 00HR.

proof.text:
Write $\operatorname{Sing}C=V(J)$, and let $s_1,\ldots,s_r$ be its minimal singular primes contained in $Q$; there are finitely many by [lem-sc-finite-minimal-primes-over-ideal]. If $s_i\subsetneq Q$, appending this strict inclusion to a chain realizing its finite height shows $\operatorname{ht}s_i<\operatorname{ht}Q\leq h$. Hence $s_i\cap B

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, Claim 5.2, Cases 1–3 and their contractions, printed pp.10–11.

proof.text: We claim $T[1/b]$ is regular. For a prime $P\subset T$ avoiding $b$, contract it to $s\subseteq Q$ in $C$. If $C_s$ were singular, [lem-weil-pbc-prime-contains-minimal-prime] would give a minimal singular prime $s_i\subseteq s$, one of those in step 11, forcing $b\in P$, a contradiction. Thus $C_s$ is regular. The map $C_s\to T_P$ is flat local with regular closed fibre: the fibre is a localization of a geometrically regular fibre of $C_Q\to T$ (step 10), so it is regular by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-of-regular-ring]. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre] to get regularity of $T_P$. Localization preserves Noetherianity by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian], proving the claim. This pointwise argument avoids an unstated comparison of singular ideals under completion.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, Claim 5.2, choice of nonzero b and regularity after inverting b, printed p.11; pointwise regular-fibre calculation.

proof.text: The map $\widehat\alpha:\widehat A\to T$ is faithfully flat (step 10). By [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-surjective-spectrum], every prime $P$ of $\widehat A$ avoiding $b$ lifts to a prime of $T$, also avoiding $b$. The resulting local map is flat, and its target is regular by step 12. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-flat-under-regular] gives regularity of $\widehat A_P$. Every prime of $L\otimes_B\widehat A$ avoids the nonzero $b$, and localization preserves regularity by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-of-regular-ring]. Hence $L\otimes_B\widehat{B_{\mathfrak q}}$ is regular. We have proved this for every finite $L/K$ and every $\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak p$. Step 6 now makes $L\otimes_K(K\otimes_R\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}})$ regular for every finite $L/K$, in particular for every finite purely inseparable extension. By [def-weil-pbc-g-ring], the generic fibre of $R_{\mathfrak p}\to\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}$ is geometrically regular. Step 4 treats every nongeneric fibre; the completion map is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-faithfully-flat]. It is therefore regular.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, Claim 5.2, final faithfully flat descent, printed p.11, followed by the finite-extension generic-fibre test.

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-g-ring-maximal-ideal-criterion], the local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a G-ring, since its only maximal-local completion map is the regular map of step 13. Then [lem-per-semilocal-g-ring-j2] makes $R_{\mathfrak p}$ quasi-excellent. It is universally catenary by the definition in [def-exc-excellent-ring]: if $D$ is generated by $d_1,\ldots,d_t$ over $R_{\mathfrak p}$, let $D_0$ be the $R$-subalgebra generated by these elements. The canonical map $(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}D_0\to D$ is surjective by the generators and injective since the denominators are already units in $D$. Between two primes surviving a localization every intermediate prime also survives, so the saturated chains and their lengths agree. Universal catenarity of $R$ therefore supplies it for $R_{\mathfrak p}$. Thus $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is excellent. At $\mathfrak p=0$, the local ring is the field $K$, excellent by [lem-exc-fields-excellent].

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 2, Claim 5.2, excellence conclusion, printed pp.10–11; Stacks 07PT, 07QT and 07QW.

proof.text: Finally fix $L$ and $\mathfrak q\subset B_L$ of height at most $h$, and put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$. Apply [lem-exc-dimension-formula-universally-catenary-finite-type-domain] to the finite extension of domains $R\subset B_L$: its fraction field extension and its residue field extension at $\mathfrak q$ are algebraic, so both transcendence degrees are zero and $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q\leq h$. Hence $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is excellent by step 14. The algebra $B_L\otimes_R R_{\mathfrak p}$ is finite, hence finite type over this ring, and $(B_L)_{\mathfrak q}$ is its localization. Apply [lem-exc-finite-type-localization-excellent] to obtain excellence of $(B_L)_{\mathfrak q}$. This includes height zero, where the localizations are fields.

source.place: Theorem 5.1 Step 3, low-height finite-normalization consequence printed p.13; Stacks 02IJ and 07QU.
